How to use this file

The Other Direction

Part 1 asked why a patient bleeds. Part 2 asks why a patient clots. The same cascade, the same laboratory tests, read for the opposite failure — and one shared molecule, von Willebrand factor, causing a bleeding disease in Part 1 and a clotting disease here.

Abbreviations used in this file TMA thrombotic microangiopathy — the umbrella term for small-vessel thrombosis with red cell destruction · TTP thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura · HUS hemolytic uremic syndrome · aHUS atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome · MAHA microangiopathic hemolytic anemia · ADAMTS13 the enzyme that cleaves von Willebrand factor multimers · VWF von Willebrand factor · VTE venous thromboembolism · DVT deep vein thrombosis · PE pulmonary embolism · FVL factor V Leiden · APS / APLA antiphospholipid (antibody) syndrome · LA lupus anticoagulant · HIT heparin-induced thrombocytopenia · LMWH low-molecular-weight heparin · DOAC direct oral anticoagulant · PF4 platelet factor 4 · SRA serotonin release assay · OCP oral contraceptive pill · HRT hormone replacement therapy · dRVVT dilute Russell viper venom test · PCC prothrombin complex concentrate. A full glossary sits at the bottom of this file.
🔑 Virchow's triad — the frame for everything in this file

Three categories of risk factor for thrombosis, and every disease and drug below maps onto one of them:

  1. Endothelial cell damageSurgery, trauma, central lines, inflammation.
  2. Blood stasisImmobilisation, prolonged travel, paralysis, pregnancy.
  3. Hypercoagulable stateThe thrombophilias — inherited and acquired. This is where objectives 2 and 3 live.

Slide 17 — Virchow's triad. Thrombosis is a common problem: roughly 1–2 per 1,000 per year overall.

🧠 How common is this?
  • Some form of thrombophilia is present in roughly 25% of the general population — which is the single best argument that finding a thrombophilia does not by itself explain a clot.
  • About 60% of patients presenting with a deep vein thrombosis will have some underlying thrombophilia.
  • Overall incidence is 1–2 per 1,000 per year, rising steeply with age — about 1 in 100,000 per year in children and up to 1 in 100 per year in the elderly.

LO 1 — Thrombotic microangiopathies

Objective 1

TTP, HUS and aHUS — Classifying the Microangiopathies

A thrombotic microangiopathy is small-vessel thrombosis that shreds red cells as they pass. The clinical presentation of all of them overlaps heavily; the classification is by mechanism, and the mechanism decides the treatment.

Abbreviations in this section TMA thrombotic microangiopathy · TTP thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura · HUS hemolytic uremic syndrome · aHUS atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome · MAHA microangiopathic hemolytic anemia — red cells shredded in small vessels · ADAMTS13 the protease that cleaves von Willebrand factor multimers · VWF von Willebrand factor · CFH complement factor H · MCP / CD46 membrane cofactor protein — a membrane-bound complement regulator · HELLP Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets · DIC disseminated intravascular coagulation · SLE systemic lupus erythematosus · APL antiphospholipid antibodies.
🔑 Mechanistic classification — the master table
PathologyMechanismClinical disease
Systemic platelet thrombiInability to degrade large von Willebrand factor multimers (ADAMTS13)TTP
Predominantly renal, platelet–fibrin-rich thrombiShiga toxin causing endothelial cell damage (E. coli)HUS
Factor H deficiency and complement activationFamilial, or aHUS
Systemic and renal thrombiDrugs and stem cell transplant, endothelial damageFeatures of both TTP and HUS
🪝 Memory hook — systemic vs renal, platelets vs fibrin

TTP is systemic and platelet-rich — ultra-large von Willebrand factor multimers grab platelets everywhere, so the brain is involved and the presentation is neurological. HUS is renal and fibrin-rich — Shiga toxin damages glomerular endothelium, so the presentation is renal failure. The overlap is real, but "brain = TTP, kidney = HUS" is the correct first instinct.

TTP — the ADAMTS13 story

Incidence is 0.37 per 100,000 per year in the United States — rare, and lethal if missed.

🧠 The mechanism, step by step
  1. Endothelial cells secrete von Willebrand factor from Weibel–Palade bodies It emerges as ultra-large multimers, anchored to the cell surface.
  2. Normally, ADAMTS13 cleaves themThe enzyme binds and trims the ultra-large multimers into normal-sized ones — hemostatically useful, but not dangerous.
  3. In TTP, ADAMTS13 is absent or blockedEither a congenital deficiency (the hereditary form, Upshaw–Schulman) or an acquired IgG inhibitor — an autoantibody against the enzyme. The acquired form is far more common.
  4. Uncleaved ultra-large multimers seize plateletsThey act as enormous adhesive ropes, driving adhesion and aggregation of platelets in the microvasculature — consuming platelets and producing thrombocytopenia.
  5. Red cells are shredded on the resulting strandsThis is microangiopathic hemolytic anemia — the source of the schistocytes.

Slide 7 — TTP pathophysiology. Left: ADAMTS13 trims the multimers. Right: it cannot, and platelets pile onto the uncleaved ropes.

Slide 8 — Two routes to the same failure: congenital ADAMTS13 deficiency, or an acquired IgG inhibitor.

Slide 9 — Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia. Red cells are sheared as they squeeze past platelet-VWF strands.

⚠️ Why TTP is a medical emergency

Untreated TTP has a mortality above 90%. The treatment is plasma exchange, which simultaneously removes the inhibitory antibody and replaces ADAMTS13 — and it is started on clinical suspicion, before the ADAMTS13 level returns.

The trap: do not transfuse platelets in suspected TTP unless there is life-threatening bleeding. The thrombocytopenia is consumptive; adding platelets adds fuel to ongoing microvascular thrombosis.

🎙️ Two details on TTP that change how you read the case
  • The acquired form is the common one, and it has a characteristic age: an autoimmune antibody against ADAMTS13 typically brings a patient in during their 20s or 30s. The congenital deficiency presents much earlier.
  • You do not want zero large multimers either. ADAMTS13 is a balancing enzyme. The large multimers are the active ones that recruit platelets to a genuine injury; the disease is having only those, so platelets are recruited everywhere.

Two vocabulary notes worth having: schistocytes are described as "triangular helmet cells", and microangiopathic hemolytic anemia decodes literally — micro-angio (small vessels) -pathic (something wrong) hemolytic anemia.

HUS — Shiga toxin and the kidney

Slide 10 — HUS pathogenesis. Shiga toxin damages glomerular endothelium directly.

🔑 Etiologic classification — what is actually understood

The lecture divides these into causes we understand and causes we do not:

Etiology understoodSubtypes
1. Infection-inducedShiga toxin / Shiga-like toxin (E. coli); neuraminidase and T antigen (Streptococcus pneumoniae)
2. Disorders of complement regulationGenetic; or acquired — anti-factor-H antibodies
3. von Willebrand proteinase (ADAMTS13) deficiencyGenetic; or acquired — autoimmune, drug-induced
4. Defective cobalamin metabolismGenetic
5. QuinineDrug-induced

Etiology not understood: HIV; malignancy, radiation, chemotherapy; calcineurin inhibitors and transplantation; pregnancy, HELLP syndrome, oral contraceptives; systemic lupus erythematosus and antiphospholipid antibodies; glomerulonephropathy; familial not otherwise specified; unclassified.

🎙️ Shiga toxin HUS — the exposure, and how a toxin ends up causing clotting

The organism is enterohemorrhagic E. coli, classically O157:H7 (also Shigella dysenteriae), and the classic exposure is undercooked or contaminated meat, producing diarrhoea and then kidney failure.

The step that is easy to miss is why an infection triggers coagulation at all. The toxin kills endothelial cells directly — and dying cells activate the immune system, which releases interleukins and chemokines. Coagulation and immunity are wired together: an inflammatory signal is also a "there may be bleeding here" signal. So fibrinogen and von Willebrand factor, both acute-phase reactants, are released, and the surge of high molecular weight von Willebrand factor reproduces the same end result as TTP by a completely different route.

That acute-phase behaviour reappears twice more in these notes: it is why fibrinogen starts high in sepsis (so a falling trend matters more than one value in DIC), and why factor 8 is elevated in the acute period, making thrombophilia testing unreliable then.

aHUS — complement out of control

🧠 The complement regulation failure

The alternative complement pathway is part of innate immunity and is constitutively ticking over — it is held in check by regulatory proteins rather than being switched on by a trigger. In atypical HUS the suppression pathway is altered, so the complement pathway is continually on, and the target of that continual attack is the patient's own endothelium.

The defects are in complement factor H (CFH), complement factor I, membrane cofactor protein (MCP/CD46), and thrombomodulin.

Slide 11 — aHUS. Loss of complement suppression leaves the alternative pathway continually active.

Slide 12 — aHUS classification.

Slide 13 — aHUS genetics and transplant outcome.

⚠️ From the speaker notes — why the genetics matter before transplant

The recurrence rate after renal transplantation is so high that children must be genetically tested before receiving a kidney. The reason is mechanistic: if the defective complement regulator is made in the liver (factor H, factor I), a new kidney enters the same hostile circulation and is attacked in turn. If the defect is in a membrane-bound regulator made by the kidney itself (MCP/CD46), a transplanted kidney brings its own working copy and does far better.

Targeted treatment is complement blockade with eculizumab, an anti-C5 antibody — which is why establishing complement as the mechanism changes management, not just the label.

Slide 14 — Recognising HUS. Diarrhoeal prodrome, pneumococcal infection, or neither — the third branch triggers a full aHUS workup.

🎙️ What complement actually does — and how that becomes a clotting disease

Complement was only touched on in the white cell lecture, so the bridge is worth spelling out. It has two jobs:

  • Opsonisation. Complement proteins coat a target and mark it for destruction, making it far easier for neutrophils and macrophages to recognise and phagocytose.
  • The membrane attack complex (MAC). Complement assembles a pore that lyses the target cell outright.

Now run that without a brake. Unregulated complement binds the patient's own cells, and the membrane attack complex destroys their endothelium. Destroyed endothelium exposes collagen and tissue factor — the exact trigger from Part 1 — and coagulation is switched on. That is the mechanistic link between an immune defect and a thrombotic disease.

Hence the pattern the lecture describes: a patient carries a regulatory mutation and is fine for years, until something triggers the system — and because the feedback that would switch it off is broken, it keeps amplifying itself. Named triggers include HIV, cancer, transplantation, tacrolimus, and pregnancy — including HELLP syndrome (Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets), associated with pre-eclampsia and eclampsia.

🎙️ Why plasma exchange is the answer in TTP — it does two things at once

The reason plasma exchange is first line, rather than simply infusing plasma:

  1. The plasma you give back replaces ADAMTS13Supplying the missing enzyme.
  2. The plasma you remove takes the antibody with itStripping out the autoantibody that was neutralising the patient's own enzyme.

Infusion alone would only do the first. Immunosuppression is added when the patient is likely to relapse. And the prognostic point on aHUS genetics: a factor H mutation carries a high rate of recurrence and of death or end-stage renal disease, whereas other mutations recur far less — which is what makes the genotype worth knowing, both for treatment and for family counselling and screening.

🪝 The single most useful discriminator: the clotting times

In every thrombotic microangiopathy the PT and aPTT are normal, because the clotting factors are not being consumed — the problem is platelets and endothelium. In DIC they are both prolonged and fibrinogen falls. If you are handed schistocytes plus thrombocytopenia, the coagulation panel is what separates the microangiopathies from DIC, and it takes one look.

Q: A 17-year-old woman presents with bruising, fever, confusion, a platelet count of 14,000/µL and schistocytes on the smear. PT and aPTT are normal, fibrinogen is normal. What is the diagnosis, what is the enzyme defect, and what is the treatment?

Answer

Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura. The combination of neurological change, thrombocytopenia and microangiopathic hemolytic anemia with normal clotting times is the classic picture — and normal PT, aPTT and fibrinogen is what excludes DIC.

The defect is ADAMTS13 — deficient or, more often, blocked by an acquired IgG inhibitor. Without it, ultra-large von Willebrand factor multimers are not cleaved and recruit platelets into systemic microthrombi.

Treatment is urgent plasma exchange, started on suspicion rather than waiting for the ADAMTS13 result. Do not give platelets unless there is life-threatening bleeding.

Q: A 4-year-old develops acute kidney injury, thrombocytopenia and a hemolytic anemia with no preceding diarrhoea. Stool studies are negative for Shiga toxin. Why does establishing the mechanism change management, and why must this be sorted out before any transplant?

Answer

This is the third branch of the recognition algorithm — no diarrhoeal prodrome and no pneumococcal infection — so a full investigation for alternative causes is required, and the leading candidate is atypical HUS from a complement regulation defect (factor H, factor I, membrane cofactor protein, thrombomodulin).

It changes management because aHUS has a targeted therapy — complement blockade with eculizumab — whereas typical Shiga toxin HUS is managed supportively.

It matters before transplant because the recurrence rate is very high, which is why the notes state children must be tested first. If the faulty regulator is a circulating protein made in the liver, the new kidney meets the same unregulated complement and is attacked; if the defect is in a membrane-bound renal protein, the graft supplies its own working copy.

LO 2 — Inherited thrombophilias

Objective 2 · part 1

Inherited Thrombophilias

Two mechanisms, and only two: either you have too little of an anticoagulant or too much (or too resistant) a procoagulant. Every inherited thrombophilia sorts into one of those buckets, and the bucket predicts how dangerous it is.

Abbreviations in this section FVL factor V Leiden — the mutated factor 5 that resists protein C · R506Q the common factor V Leiden mutation, named for the amino acid change · G20210A the common prothrombin mutation, named for the DNA position · 3′ UTR three-prime untranslated region — the non-coding tail of a messenger RNA · mRNA messenger ribonucleic acid · VTE venous thromboembolism · DVT deep vein thrombosis · AT III antithrombin III · OCP oral contraceptive pill · Lp(a) lipoprotein(a).
🔑 The full list, split by mechanism
🚫

Deficit in antithrombotic proteins

Lose a brake. Rarer, but much higher risk per patient.

  • Protein C deficiency
  • Protein S deficiency
  • Antithrombin III deficiency
⚡

Excessive activation of prothrombotic factors

Push the accelerator. Far more common, lower risk each.

  • Factor V Leiden mutation
  • Prothrombin G20210A mutation
  • Dysfibrinogenemia

Slide 20 — The cascade with its brakes drawn in. Antithrombin III on thrombin and factor 10a; activated protein C with protein S on factors 5a and 8a.

Protein C and protein S deficiency

  • Overall these protein deficiencies are rare.
  • Protein S deficiency appears to be worse than protein C deficiency, and having both together is worse still.
  • Homozygous protein C or S deficiency causes potentially fatal purpura fulminans shortly after birth — widespread dermal microvascular thrombosis with skin necrosis. It is a neonatal emergency.
  • Testing: protein C activity assay; free protein S antigen plus protein S activity assay.

Slide 22 — Protein C and S deficiency. Homozygous deficiency presents as neonatal purpura fulminans.

🎙️ Purpura fulminans — why the skin bleeds in a clotting disease

The name looks contradictory until you follow the mechanism. Homozygous protein C or S deficiency produces disseminated clotting in the capillaries; the occluded capillaries then rupture, and blood leaks into the surrounding tissue. The purpura is the consequence of the thrombosis, not of a bleeding tendency.

Practical replacement differs between the two, which is worth knowing: a protein C concentrate exists, whereas for protein S you give plasma. Testing is by activity assays, with antigen assays available alongside.

Antithrombin III deficiency

  • Relatively rare as a genetic disorder — under 0.5% of the population.
  • Homozygous antithrombin deficiency is not compatible with life.
  • Antithrombin III is a small protein and can be easily lost. Proteinuria (nephrotic syndrome) and chest tube drainage can both cause an acquired deficiency — so a low level does not automatically mean an inherited disorder.
  • Reduced effectiveness of heparin occurs, because heparin works through antithrombin. This is the classic explanation for "heparin resistance".
  • Detected by a functional assay.
🎙️ The full list of ways antithrombin gets lost — and how to rescue heparin

Antithrombin is a small protein, so anything that leaks protein depletes it. The causes named in the recording go beyond the slide:

  • Nephrotic syndrome — the kidneys leak protein
  • Chest tube drainage
  • Protein-losing enteropathies
  • Severe heart failure

And the management step that follows: heparin increases antithrombin's enzymatic activity — that is its entire mechanism. So in a patient receiving large doses of heparin with no effect, the answer is not more heparin but antithrombin III supplementation, so that the heparin can work to its full effect.

Factor V Leiden — the common one

🔑 The most common thrombophilia
  • Present in about 5% of Caucasians, and accounts for 20–30% of venous thromboembolism events.
  • The common mutation is R506Q, detected by molecular testing.
  • Homozygotes carry a substantially higher thrombosis risk than heterozygotes.
  • Mechanism: the mutation prevents deactivation of factor V by protein C — "activated protein C resistance". The net effect is similar to protein C deficiency.
  • Protein C deficiency and factor V Leiden can coexist, and together the venous thromboembolism risk is increased further.

Slide 24 — Factor V Leiden. The mutated factor 5 resists cleavage by activated protein C.

🪝 Memory hook — two ways to fail the same reaction

The reaction is activated protein C cleaves factor 5a. You can break it by removing the scissors (protein C deficiency) or by armour-plating the paper (factor V Leiden). Same downstream result: factor 5a survives, thrombin generation runs on. That is why the lecture says the effect is "similar overall" — and why having both is additive.

Prothrombin G20210A mutation

  • Prevalence 2.3% in Caucasians and 0.5% in African-Americans.
  • Increased activity of prothrombin causes a more hypercoagulable state.
  • G20210A is the common mutation, found by molecular testing.
  • The elegant part of the mechanism: the mutation is in the 3′ untranslated region — it does not change the protein at all. It increases pre-messenger-RNA stability, so more prothrombin is made. More substrate, more thrombin.

Slide 25 — Prothrombin G20210A. A 3′ untranslated region mutation that raises prothrombin levels.

🎙️ Two acquired entries worth expanding
  • Essential thrombocythemia — a myeloproliferative disorder producing a persistently high platelet count. At a million or more, that is, in the lecture's phrase, "a lot of fuel there to generate a clot." Distinguish it from a reactive thrombocytosis, which is temporary.
  • Oral contraceptives plus smoking is called out specifically as carrying a very high clotting risk — and, importantly, a reversible one. Stopping both may remove the need for anticoagulation altogether, which is why identifying the combination matters more than treating around it.

Lipoprotein(a) sits slightly apart: it is associated mainly with atherosclerotic disease, with a possible additional thrombotic contribution.

🧠 The acquired thrombophilias, for contrast

Listed on the same slide, and worth holding alongside the inherited list:

  • Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome — lupus anticoagulant, anti-cardiolipin, anti-β2-glycoprotein-I. Gets its own objective below.
  • Elevated platelet count or fibrinogen.
  • Elevated levels of factors 8, 9, 11.
  • Malignancy.
  • Hormones — oral contraceptives, estrogen, pregnancy.
  • Lipoprotein(a).

Slide 30 — Summary of thrombophilias. Every named defect placed on one diagram of the protein C / thrombin axis.

🎙️ Where hyperhomocysteinemia fits on the summary diagram

The summary figure shows hyperhomocysteinemia feeding into the protein C axis, and the reason is simple: high homocysteine inhibits protein C. So it converges on the same end result as protein C deficiency and as factor V Leiden — factor 5a is not switched off, and thrombin generation runs on.

That is the unifying way to read the whole diagram: three different lesions, one shared failure — remove the scissors (protein C or S deficiency), armour-plate the target (factor V Leiden), or poison the scissors (homocysteine).

Q: A patient with nephrotic syndrome fails to achieve a therapeutic aPTT despite escalating heparin doses. What is the likely explanation?

Answer

Acquired antithrombin III deficiency from urinary protein loss. Antithrombin III is a small protein that is easily lost, and proteinuria is named explicitly as a cause (as is chest tube drainage).

It matters because heparin works by activating antithrombin III — heparin has essentially no anticoagulant action of its own. With little antithrombin present, more heparin achieves little: the classic picture of heparin resistance. Management is to check an antithrombin level and use an agent that does not depend on it (for example a direct thrombin inhibitor), or to replace antithrombin.

Q: Explain why the prothrombin G20210A mutation causes thrombophilia even though it does not alter a single amino acid of the prothrombin protein.

Answer

Because it is a regulatory mutation, not a coding one. G20210A sits in the 3′ untranslated region of the gene and increases pre-messenger-RNA stability. A more stable transcript is translated more, so the patient makes more prothrombin.

The protein itself is entirely normal — there is simply more substrate available for the cascade to convert into thrombin, which shifts the hemostatic balance toward clotting. This is why the diagnosis is made by molecular testing rather than by a functional assay: a protein activity test would look normal.

LO 2 — Acquired thrombophilia

Objective 2 · part 2

Antiphospholipid Syndrome and the Lupus Anticoagulant

The most important acquired thrombophilia, and the one with the most confusing name in hematology. The lecture calls it a double misnomer, and unpacking why is the fastest route to understanding the laboratory testing.

Abbreviations in this section APS antiphospholipid syndrome · APLA antiphospholipid antibody · LA lupus anticoagulant · dRVVT dilute Russell viper venom test — a phospholipid-dependent clotting assay · aPTT activated partial thromboplastin time · anti-β2-GP1 anti-beta-2-glycoprotein-1 antibody · IgG / IgM immunoglobulin G / immunoglobulin M — antibody classes · VDRL / RPR Venereal Disease Research Laboratory / rapid plasma reagin — the non-treponemal syphilis tests, which use a cardiolipin antigen.
⚠️ "Lupus anticoagulant" — a double misnomer
  1. Not lupusPatients with a lupus anticoagulant do not necessarily have lupus — about 8% may develop it later.
  2. Not an anticoagulantIt increases coagulation time in vitro (which is where the name came from) but increases the risk of thrombosis in vivo. The test tube and the patient point in opposite directions.
🧠 Why the paradox exists

The clotting assays are run on a phospholipid surface. The antibody binds phospholipid, so in the tube it competes with the clotting complexes for a limited amount of surface and the reaction is slowed — a prolonged clotting time. In the patient, phospholipid is not limiting; instead the antibodies activate endothelium and platelets and interfere with natural anticoagulant pathways, which promotes thrombosis.

This is also the key to the confirmatory test: because the inhibition is phospholipid-dependent, adding extra phospholipid corrects the clotting time. Adding normal plasma does not.

🎙️ How much overlap is there really between lupus and the lupus anticoagulant?

Less than the name implies. The relationship is a Venn diagram with partial overlap:

  • You can have lupus without a lupus anticoagulant.
  • You can have a lupus anticoagulant without meeting criteria for lupus.
  • The lupus anticoagulant is not part of the diagnostic criteria for lupus at all.

Patients with lupus certainly can develop one — but the two are separate entities that were linked by the order of discovery, not by definition. The name has simply stuck.

Testing

  1. Mixing studyPatient plasma plus normal plasma. A lupus anticoagulant does not correct — it is an inhibitor, not a deficiency.
  2. aPTT assay and/or dilute Russell viper venom test (dRVVT)Both are phospholipid-dependent clotting assays. The dRVVT is more specific for a lupus anticoagulant.
  3. Confirm with excess phospholipidAdding extra phospholipid corrects the prolongation — proving the inhibitor is directed at phospholipid rather than at a specific factor.
  4. Immunoassays for the individual antibodiesSee the list below.

Slide 28 — Back to the mixing study. A factor deficiency corrects with normal plasma; antiphospholipid antibodies do not.

🔑 The other antiphospholipid antibodies
  • Anti-cardiolipin IgG and IgM — the classic cause of a false-positive test for syphilis, because the non-treponemal syphilis tests use a cardiolipin antigen.
  • Anti-β2-glycoprotein-1 IgG and IgM.
  • Anti-phosphatidylserine.
  • Anti-prothrombin — note the exception: at a high level this may lead to a hemorrhagic disorder rather than thrombosis, by clearing prothrombin from the circulation.

Diagnostic criteria — one clinical plus one laboratory

Clinical criteria (at least one)Laboratory criteria
a. Vascular thrombosis — arterial, venous, or small vessel. Not superficial venous thrombosis.

b. Pregnancy morbidity, any one of:
  i. Three or more unexplained consecutive miscarriages before the 10th week of gestation.
  ii. One or more unexplained deaths of a morphologically normal fetus at or beyond the 10th week.
  iii. One or more premature births of a morphologically normal neonate before the 34th week due to eclampsia, severe pre-eclampsia, or placental insufficiency.		 Prolonged clotting times that do not correct on mixing with plasma, but do correct with extra phospholipid.

Persistent — positive on two occasions at least 12 weeks apart.

Timing relative to the event: 12 weeks to 5 years.
🎙️ Having the antibody is not having the syndrome

Stated plainly: more people have antiphospholipid antibodies than have antiphospholipid syndrome. The syndrome requires both a clinical and a laboratory criterion — which is why the antibody alone is not a diagnosis.

And the management consequence, which is the part most often got wrong: a patient with antiphospholipid antibodies but no thrombosis and no pregnancy morbidity is generally not anticoagulated. Treatment follows the syndrome, not the serology.

The reason for the 12-week rule, in the lecturer's own terms: after a recent clot, during an infection, or in any severely ill patient, you can transiently form antibodies that look like they bind phospholipid, and these disappear once the patient recovers. A genuine antiphospholipid antibody gives a strong reaction and persists.

🪝 The "12 weeks apart" rule is the whole point

Antiphospholipid antibodies appear transiently after infections and with some drugs. A single positive result during an acute illness means little. Requiring persistence over at least 12 weeks is what separates a real, thrombosis-associated syndrome from a passing epiphenomenon. Notice the number of events also scales with gestational age — three early losses, but only one after 10 weeks, because a late loss is a far rarer and more specific event.

Q: A woman with three first-trimester miscarriages has a prolonged aPTT. She has never bled abnormally. The mixing study does not correct. Should she be given fresh frozen plasma before her next procedure?

Answer

No. This is a lupus anticoagulant, and the prolonged aPTT is an in-vitro artefact: the antibody competes for the phospholipid surface the assay depends on. Clinically she is at risk of thrombosis, not bleeding — the second half of the "double misnomer".

Confirm by showing the prolongation corrects with added phospholipid (and with a dilute Russell viper venom test), then check anti-cardiolipin and anti-β2-glycoprotein-1 antibodies. Diagnosis requires persistence on repeat testing at least 12 weeks apart. With three unexplained consecutive losses before 10 weeks she meets the clinical criterion, so a persistent laboratory finding would establish antiphospholipid syndrome.

Q: A patient has a positive non-treponemal syphilis test but treponemal-specific testing is negative. What hematological condition should you consider, and why does the false positive happen?

Answer

Antiphospholipid syndrome, specifically anti-cardiolipin antibodies.

The non-treponemal syphilis tests (VDRL, RPR) use a cardiolipin-based antigen. A patient whose own antibodies are directed against cardiolipin will bind that antigen and produce a biological false-positive. The treponemal-specific test, which uses actual Treponema pallidum antigens, stays negative.

Follow up with lupus anticoagulant testing and anti-β2-glycoprotein-1 antibodies, repeated at 12 weeks to establish persistence.

LO 3 — Antiplatelet agents

Objective 3 · part 1

Antiplatelet Agents — Aspirin and Clopidogrel

Abbreviations in this section COX cyclo-oxygenase, also called prostaglandin H synthase — aspirin's target · TXA2 thromboxane A2 — the platelet-recruiting mediator aspirin blocks · P2Y12 the platelet adenosine diphosphate receptor blocked by clopidogrel · ADP adenosine diphosphate · NSAID non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug.

The lecture opens the drug section with a second matching exercise: which drugs inhibit platelets, and which inhibit clotting factors? Aspirin and clopidogrel inhibit platelets. Heparin and warfarin inhibit clotting factors. That split is the organising principle for everything below.

🔑 Aspirin
  • An irreversible inhibitor of prostaglandin H synthase (cyclo-oxygenase). Because the inhibition is irreversible and platelets have no nucleus and cannot make new enzyme, the effect lasts the lifetime of the platelet — recovery requires new platelets over roughly 7–10 days.
  • Blocking the enzyme prevents thromboxane A2 synthesis, and thromboxane A2 is what platelets use to recruit and activate one another.
  • Generally the first-line anticoagulant for mildly increased thrombosis risk.
  • Recall from Part 1: aspirin produces the same aggregometry pattern as an arachidonic acid / thromboxane pathway defect, so always ask about it before diagnosing a platelet function disorder.

Slide 35 — Aspirin. Irreversible cyclo-oxygenase inhibition; the platelet cannot make new enzyme.

🎙️ Why aspirin causes ulcers, and why it has to be taken daily

Aspirin blocks prostaglandin H synthase, which sits upstream of all the prostaglandins — not only thromboxane A2. Some of the others are gastrointestinal protective. Knocking those out too is why chronic aspirin and other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs cause ulcers: the therapeutic effect and the main side effect come from the same enzyme.

And the apparent contradiction in dosing: aspirin is irreversible, yet it is taken every day. Both are true because the marrow keeps making new platelets. Each dose permanently disables the platelets circulating at that moment; tomorrow's fresh platelets are untouched. Stop the drug and full function returns over 7–10 days, as the whole population turns over.

Historical aside: the analgesic properties of willow bark were known long before aspirin was synthesised in the late 1800s.

🔑 Clopidogrel
  • Blocks the platelet activation pathway by irreversibly inhibiting the P2Y12 receptor — the adenosine diphosphate (ADP) chemoreceptor.
  • Similar drugs: prasugrel, ticlopidine.
  • The important limitation, stated directly: not particularly useful when platelets are normal and other factors contribute to the thrombosis. An antiplatelet drug is the wrong tool for a factor-driven venous clot.

Slide 36 — Clopidogrel. Irreversible P2Y12 (ADP receptor) blockade.

🎙️ Why a patient might be on aspirin and clopidogrel at once

They hit different platelet receptors — aspirin removes thromboxane A2 signalling, clopidogrel blocks the P2Y12 adenosine diphosphate receptor — so the effects are synergistic rather than redundant.

The clinical setting named in the recording is coronary stents, including in young patients with abnormal cardiac anatomy. Stents are highly sensitive to platelet clumping, so dual antiplatelet therapy is what keeps them patent. This is the archetypal platelet-rich, arterial problem, and it is why an antiplatelet regimen is right here and wrong for a deep vein thrombosis.

🪝 Memory hook — arterial versus venous

Arterial thrombi are platelet-rich (high shear, "white clots") — so antiplatelet drugs are the mainstay for coronary and cerebrovascular disease. Venous thrombi are fibrin- and red-cell-rich (low flow, "red clots") — so anticoagulants are the mainstay for deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism. That is the mechanistic reason behind the lecture's warning that clopidogrel is not useful when the platelets are not the problem.

Q: A patient stops aspirin today for surgery in three days. Is that long enough, and why does the answer depend on aspirin being an irreversible inhibitor?

Answer

No — aspirin is usually stopped 7–10 days before surgery. Aspirin is an irreversible inhibitor of prostaglandin H synthase, and a platelet has no nucleus, so it cannot synthesise replacement enzyme. Every platelet aspirin has touched stays inhibited for the rest of its life.

Recovery therefore depends entirely on the marrow producing new platelets, which takes roughly the platelet lifespan of 7–10 days — not on the drug clearing from plasma, which happens within hours.

The same fact explains a laboratory finding from Part 1: aspirin produces the same aggregometry pattern as an arachidonic acid / thromboxane A2 pathway defect, so a platelet function study must be repeated after 7–10 days off the drug before that diagnosis can be made.

Q: A patient with a first unprovoked deep vein thrombosis is started on clopidogrel. What is wrong with this choice?

Answer

Clopidogrel is an antiplatelet drug, and the lecture states plainly that it is not particularly useful when platelets are normal and other factors contribute to the thrombosis.

A deep vein thrombosis is a venous, fibrin-rich clot formed in low flow — it is driven by the coagulation cascade, not by platelet activation. Blocking the P2Y12 adenosine diphosphate receptor does little about that.

The correct choice is an anticoagulant — a heparin, warfarin, or a direct oral anticoagulant. Antiplatelet agents belong to the arterial, platelet-rich side of the disease: coronary and cerebrovascular thrombosis.

LO 3 — Heparins

Objective 3 · part 2

Heparin, Low-Molecular-Weight Heparin, and HIT

Abbreviations in this section UFH unfractionated heparin · LMWH low-molecular-weight heparin · AT III antithrombin III — the protein heparin works through · aPTT activated partial thromboplastin time · anti-Xa anti-factor 10a activity, an alternative heparin assay · HIT heparin-induced thrombocytopenia · PF4 platelet factor 4 — the platelet protein that binds heparin to form the HIT antigen · SRA serotonin release assay · 4T score Thrombocytopenia, Timing, Thrombosis, oTher cause · BID / Q12H twice daily.
🔑 Unfractionated heparin
  • Activates antithrombin III — it has essentially no intrinsic anticoagulant activity of its own. This is why antithrombin deficiency causes heparin resistance.
  • Monitored by aPTT; therapeutic range is 1.5–2.5 times normal.
  • Or by anti-factor 10a levels — therapeutic 0.3–0.7 U/mL.
  • Hepatic clearance — contrast with the renally-cleared low-molecular-weight heparins.
  • Reversed by protamine sulfate.
  • Drawbacks: bleeding, osteoporosis, close monitoring required, and the risk of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.
  • A piece of trivia the lecture keeps because it is memorable: one unit of heparin (about 0.002 mg) is the quantity required to keep 1 mL of cat's blood fluid for 24 hours at 0 °C.
🎙️ The tail — why aPTT monitors unfractionated heparin but not the low-molecular-weight ones

This is the single best mechanistic explanation in the anticoagulant section, and it is not on the slides. Heparin is a chain of sugars, and it comes in different lengths — much like von Willebrand factor multimers.

  • To inactivate thrombin, antithrombin and thrombin must be bridged together, and it is the heparin molecule's long tail that provides that bridge. Only a long chain can do it.
  • To inactivate factor 10a, no bridge is needed — antithrombin does it well on its own once heparin has activated it. A short chain is enough.

Everything follows from that asymmetry:

AgentAnti-thrombin effectAnti-factor-10a effectSo monitor with
Unfractionated heparin (long tail)StrongStrongaPTT works — it senses the thrombin effect. Anti-Xa also valid
LMWH, fondaparinux (short)WeakStrongAnti-factor 10a only — the aPTT has little to detect

A practice note: anti-factor 10a has largely replaced the aPTT even for unfractionated heparin in many laboratories. When a modern chart says "therapeutic heparin level", it usually means the anti-Xa result.

Unfractionated heparinLow-molecular-weight heparinFondaparinux
ExamplesHeparinEnoxaparin, dalteparinFondaparinux — a pentasaccharide

Slide 38 — Low-molecular-weight heparin and fondaparinux. Renally cleared, predictable, lower HIT risk.

🎙️ What makes unfractionated heparin worth its inconveniences

The drawbacks are real, but the recording is clear that heparin "has a lot of good things going for it" — and the reasons matter when choosing an agent:

  • Short half-life. Adjust the dose and the patient is at the new steady state within hours. That control is why it is the agent for unstable patients.
  • It has a real antidote. Protamine sulfate reverses it quickly — which is exactly what cardiopulmonary bypass requires, where a patient is fully heparinised on the circuit and must be reversed on coming off.
  • Hepatic clearance — so, unlike the low-molecular-weight heparins, it is the safer choice in renal impairment. Dose-adjust in liver disease instead.

The cost is that it is intravenous with a short half-life, so it is essentially an inpatient-only drug. Low-molecular-weight heparin's predictable pharmacokinetics and once- or twice-daily subcutaneous dosing are what make outpatient anticoagulation possible at all.

Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia

⚠️ The counterintuitive core of HIT

HIT is a prothrombotic state. The platelet count falls, but the danger is thrombosis, not bleeding — new venous and arterial clots at a ratio of roughly 4:1 venous to arterial. Every management error below follows from forgetting this.

PatternTimingFeatures
Typical5–14 days after first exposurePlatelet count falls by >50% or below 100,000/µL; new thrombosis while on heparin
Rapid onset (some)Within hours of re-exposureOccurs when there has been heparin exposure within the previous 100 days — antibody is already present
Delayed onset (few)Several days after heparin has been stoppedEasy to miss, because the drug is already gone

Slide 39 — HIT. Antibodies against the heparin–platelet factor 4 complex activate platelets.

🎙️ Why HIT takes 5–14 days, and why past HIT closes off the whole class

The delay is an immune delay. Heparin binds platelets and forms a complex with platelet factor 4; the patient's immune system then has to recognise that complex and manufacture antibodies against it, which takes 5–14 days. The antibody then binds platelets and activates them — which is why the platelet count falls (they are being consumed into clots) and why the patient clots rather than bleeds.

That also explains the variants: with pre-existing antibody from exposure in the past 100 days there is no immunisation delay, so onset is within hours.

And the consequence for the future: once a patient has had HIT, low-molecular-weight heparin and fondaparinux are closed off too. They are structurally related, and the existing antibody can cross-react with them. A lower risk of causing HIT is not the same as being safe once the antibody exists.

🔑 The 4T score — pre-test probability
Criterion2 points1 point0 points
Thrombocytopenia>50% fall, or nadir 20–100 ×109/L30–50% fall, or nadir 10–20 ×109/LFall <30%, or nadir <10 ×109/L
Timing of the fallClear onset days 5–10; or <1 day if heparin exposure within the past 100 daysConsistent with immunisation but not clear (e.g. missing counts), or onset after day 10Fall too early, without recent heparin exposure
Thrombosis or other sequelaeNew thrombosis; skin necrosis; post-heparin-bolus acute systemic reactionProgressive or recurrent thrombosis; erythematous skin lesions; suspected but unproven thrombosisNone
oTher cause for thrombocytopeniaNo other cause evidentPossible other cause evidentDefinite other cause present

Score 6–8 = high · 4–5 = intermediate · 0–3 = low pre-test probability.

🎙️ The 4T score is a decision rule, not a description

The score exists to tell you whether to test at all:

Pre-test probabilityWhat to do
High (6–8)Treat as HIT. Stop the heparin, start an alternative. Do not wait for a result
Low (0–3)Do not send the test. It is not HIT — and a false positive will cause harm
Intermediate (4–5)This is where testing actually helps decide

The reason low probability means don't test: plenty of people have the anti-PF4 antibody without having HIT. Sending the assay indiscriminately generates positives that then force you to stop heparin in patients who never had the disease.

How to read the result once you have it:

  • Negative is genuinely useful — the immunoassay is very sensitive, so a negative result essentially rules HIT out.
  • Positive leaves you stuck — it is not specific, so you must treat as HIT while sending the serotonin release assay. That test takes the patient's platelets, adds heparin, and measures whether serotonin is released. It is complex and run only in reference laboratories, so the answer is not quick — which is precisely why clinical impression is the most important element.

Diagnosis and testing strategy

  • Clinical impression is the most important thing — stated first on the slide, ahead of any assay.
  • Characterised by anti-heparin/platelet factor 4 (PF4) antibodies, detected by an immunologic assay.
  • Serotonin release assay (SRA) — a functional test measuring actual platelet activation. More specific, and used when the immunoassay and the clinical picture disagree.
  1. Order heparin–PF4 antibodies (plasma)And stop heparin immediately if suspicion is real — do not wait for the result.
  2. Positive and matches clinical suspicion → stop testing, treat for HIT
  3. Negative and matches clinical suspicion → stop testing
  4. Result does not match clinical suspicion → send a serotonin release assay (serum)More than 24 hours after heparin was discontinued. In the meantime the patient must be on an alternative anticoagulant.
🧠 How to interpret the results honestly
  • Laboratory testing does not exclude a diagnosis of HIT. Nevertheless, the negative predictive value approaches 100% when both the serotonin release assay and the heparin–PF4 assay are negative.
  • Positive results alone do not mean the thrombocytopenia can be attributed solely to heparin — anti-PF4 antibodies are common in hospitalised patients and most do not have clinical HIT. Other co-existing etiologies must be considered.
⚠️ Treatment — and the three scenarios to avoid

HIT is a hypercoagulable state, but you cannot use any heparin compound or warfarin. Institute an alternative antithrombotic: argatroban or lepirudin (direct thrombin inhibitors).

Avoid these three:

  • Using warfarin alone — associated with gangrene. Warfarin drops protein C before it drops the procoagulant factors, transiently deepening the prothrombotic state in a patient who is already thrombosing. Venous limb gangrene is the result.
  • Using low-molecular-weight heparin — the antibody can cross-react. Lower HIT risk is not the same as safe once the antibody exists.
  • No anticoagulation at all — HIT is a prothrombotic state. The instinct to stop everything because the platelets are low is exactly wrong.

Q: A post-operative patient on unfractionated heparin has a platelet count fall from 240,000 to 85,000/µL on day 7, and develops a new deep vein thrombosis. What is the 4T score, and what are the two most important immediate actions?

Answer

4T score = 8, high probability. Thrombocytopenia: a >50% fall with a nadir between 20 and 100 ×109/L — 2 points. Timing: clear onset on day 7, within the 5–10 day window — 2 points. Thrombosis: new thrombosis — 2 points. Other cause: none evident — 2 points.

Two immediate actions: (1) stop all heparin, including flushes and heparin-bonded lines, and (2) start an alternative anticoagulant — argatroban. Send heparin–PF4 antibodies, but do not wait for the result to act.

Do not switch to low-molecular-weight heparin (cross-reactivity), do not start warfarin alone (gangrene risk from the protein C drop), and do not simply stop anticoagulation because the platelets are low.

LO 3 — Oral anticoagulants

Objective 3 · part 3

Warfarin and the Direct Oral Anticoagulants

Abbreviations in this section INR international normalised ratio — the standardised prothrombin time · PT prothrombin time · FFP fresh frozen plasma · PCC prothrombin complex concentrate · DOAC direct oral anticoagulant · Xa activated factor 10 · DTI direct thrombin inhibitor.
🔑 Warfarin — and the "1972" mnemonic
  • Oral vitamin K antagonist.
  • Prevents formation of factors 2, 7, 9, 10 and proteins C and S — the lecture's mnemonic is "1972" for the factor numbers.
  • Monitored with PT / INR.
  • Antidotes: vitamin K (oral or intravenous), fresh frozen plasma, prothrombin complex concentrates.
🎙️ Why the INR exists, and how the diet interaction actually runs

The INR was created for portability. Different laboratories use different thromboplastin reagents, so a raw prothrombin time in seconds is not comparable between hospitals. The INR is mathematically standardised so a patient's result means the same thing wherever it is measured — essential for a drug monitored lifelong across different sites.

Day-to-day adjustment is as simple as it sounds: INR too high → skip or reduce a dose; INR too low → increase the dose.

The dietary interaction is worth getting the right way round, because it is counterintuitive:

  • More dietary vitamin K → warfarin becomes LESS effective → INR falls → risk of clotting.
  • Less dietary vitamin K → effectively an OVERDOSE → INR rises → risk of bleeding.

Which is why the advice is a steady vitamin K intake, not avoidance of greens — consistency matters more than quantity.

⚠️ Warfarin's three warnings
  • Must bridge with heparin for a few days, because of protein S and C depletion. Protein C has a shorter half-life than factors 2, 9 and 10, so it disappears first — making the patient transiently more prothrombotic in the first days of therapy. This is the mechanism behind warfarin-induced skin necrosis, and behind the gangrene warning in HIT.
  • Interactions with diet and other medications — dietary vitamin K, and a long list of drug interactions through hepatic metabolism.
  • Contraindicated in pregnancy, but may be used post-partum. Warfarin crosses the placenta and is teratogenic; heparins do not cross and are the pregnancy-safe alternative.

Slide 43 — Warfarin. Vitamin K antagonist affecting factors 2, 7, 9, 10 and proteins C and S.

🪝 Why the INR rises before the patient is actually anticoagulated

The PT/INR is most sensitive to factor 7, and factor 7 has the shortest half-life of the vitamin K-dependent factors (about 6 hours). So the INR climbs within a day or two — while factor 2 (prothrombin), with a half-life around 60 hours, is still largely intact. The number looks therapeutic before the patient is. That, plus the early protein C drop, is the complete argument for heparin bridging.

Slide 44 — DOACs. Four factor 10a inhibitors and one direct thrombin inhibitor.

🎙️ What a DOAC actually is, and what happens in overdose

The cleanest one-line framing offered: a factor 10a inhibitor does what low-molecular-weight heparin does, except it is oral. That is the whole commercial proposition — no injections, no routine monitoring, rapid onset, few interactions.

The flip side is what happens when things go wrong. Because monitoring is not well established, a patient presenting with a DOAC overdose is difficult to manage: there may be no good laboratory test to tell you how much drug is on board, so management becomes empirical. Cost is the other limitation, though it should fall as these agents become generic.

The practical levers in an overdose are therefore time since the last dose and renal function, since these drugs are substantially renally cleared.

🪝 Memory hook — "-xaban" tells you the target

Rivaroxaban, apixaban, edoxaban, betrixaban — the "xa" in the stem is literally factor Xa. Dabigatran has no "xa" and is the direct thrombin inhibitor. The name carries the mechanism.

Q: Why must warfarin be bridged with heparin, and what happens if it is not?

Answer

Because warfarin blocks the vitamin K-dependent anticoagulants — proteins C and S — as well as the procoagulant factors, and protein C has a shorter half-life than factors 2, 9 and 10. In the first days of therapy protein C is gone while prothrombin is largely intact, so the patient is transiently more prothrombotic.

Without bridging, the consequences are warfarin-induced skin necrosis (classically in patients with underlying protein C deficiency) and, in a patient with HIT, venous limb gangrene.

A second reason the INR misleads early: it is driven mainly by factor 7, which has the shortest half-life of all. The INR therefore looks therapeutic days before factor 2 has fallen enough to actually protect the patient.

Q: A patient on a direct oral anticoagulant needs emergency surgery. Why is the routine coagulation panel unhelpful, and what does this lecture list as the class's key limitations?

Answer

Because laboratory monitoring of DOACs is more difficult — the PT and aPTT are calibrated for warfarin and heparin and do not reliably reflect a DOAC level. A normal PT does not prove a factor 10a inhibitor has cleared, and a mildly prolonged one does not quantify how much is present. Drug-specific assays (anti-factor 10a calibrated to the particular agent, or a dilute thrombin time for dabigatran) are required.

The limitations listed in this lecture are cost, no antidote available, and laboratory monitoring may be more difficult. Practically, the management levers are time since the last dose and renal function, since these agents are substantially renally cleared.

LO 4 — Individualised approach

Objective 4

When to Test, and How Long to Treat

Abbreviations in this section VTE venous thromboembolism · DVT deep vein thrombosis · FVL factor V Leiden · RR relative risk · OCP / HRT oral contraceptive pill / hormone replacement therapy · PV / ET polycythemia vera / essential thrombocythemia — myeloproliferative neoplasms · TAFI thrombin-activatable fibrinolysis inhibitor · FVIII factor 8.

The fourth objective asks you to design an approach rather than recall a fact. Two questions drive it: should this patient be tested for thrombophilia at all, and how long should they be anticoagulated? The answer to the second turns out to depend far more on the circumstances of the clot than on any genetic result.

🎙️ The rule that governs all of this: does the result change what you do?

Put more forcefully in the recording than on the slide: "If you're sending the test and the result doesn't impact anything you're doing, you probably didn't need to send that test." These assays cost money and, worse, generate findings that invite unnecessary lifelong therapy.

So before sending, be able to finish this sentence: if it is positive I will <do X>; if it is negative I will <do Y>. If X and Y are the same, don't send it. The two answers that legitimately justify testing are "it will change whether or how long I anticoagulate" and "it will trigger family counselling and screening".

One test escapes the timing problem entirely: genetic testing — factor V Leiden and prothrombin G20210A — can be run at any time, and only ever needs to be run once. It is expensive, and the answer will never change.

🔑 When to evaluate for thrombophilia
  • Family history of clotting
  • Young age — under 45 years
  • Absence of risk factors — no recent surgery, long flight, or malignancy
  • Recurrent thromboses
  • Unusual location — upper extremity, mesenteric vessels
  • Specific paediatric scenarios — single ventricle physiology, ventricular assist device evaluation

And the two questions the lecture insists you ask before sending anything: How are positive results used? Will they guide therapy? Is this for family counselling? If a positive result would not change what you do, the test is not indicated.

Slide 18 — Risk factors: transient, persistent, and inherited. Most clots have an acquired trigger.

TransientPersistentInherited
SurgeryObesityFactor V Leiden mutation
TraumaCancer and its therapyProthrombin gene mutation
Central linesInflammatory bowel diseaseProtein S deficiency
Pregnancy / postpartum — 1.7 per 1,000 deliveriesMyeloproliferative neoplasms — polycythemia vera, essential thrombocythemiaProtein C deficiency
Oral contraceptives / hormone replacement — relative risk 4×Nephrotic syndromeAntithrombin deficiency
Acute medical illnessParalysisDysfibrinogenemia (rare)
Disseminated intravascular coagulationAntiphospholipid antibody syndrome
Immobilisation
Prolonged travel — 4+ hours; 1 in 4,600 flights
🎙️ Where clots form, and the two things every admitted patient gets assessed for

Stasis is where clots start. The mechanism is mundane: veins are pumped by the surrounding muscles and kept unidirectional by one-way valves, so blood only moves up the leg when you do. When it stops moving, platelets come into contact with each other and red cells settle — add dehydration on a long flight and that is a deep vein thrombosis.

Clots therefore form in dependent areas, usually the legs. Which is why an unusual site is a red flag worth testing: mesenteric vessels, upper extremity, or cerebral venous sinus.

Two practical points that follow:

  • Every adult admission includes a thromboprophylaxis decision — compression stockings, prophylactic heparin, or both.
  • Central lines must be locked with heparin. The body treats indwelling plastic as foreign: platelets adhere to it and fibrin forms on it. (They are also a major infection route, which is the other reason not to leave one in past its usefulness.)

And the reason any of this matters: the deep vein thrombosis itself is painful, but what you actually dread is that clot dislodging into the lungs. A pulmonary embolism can kill the patient.

Pregnancy deserves its own note — the hypercoagulability is deliberate physiology, protecting against haemorrhage at delivery, and it peaks postpartum, when the placental bed must clot down.

Risk stratification — the numbers that decide duration

🔑 Recurrence risk in the first year, by the circumstances of the clot
Situation at the time of thrombosisExampleRecurrence risk in the first year
Major transient risk factorProlonged bedrest in hospital, surgery3%
Minor reversible risk factorOral contraceptive, long airplane trip5%
Unprovoked venous thromboembolism, or a persistent risk factorNo identifiable trigger; ongoing malignancy10%

This is the core of objective 4: determine which risk factors were present at the time of the thrombosis, because that — more than any genetic test — predicts recurrence and therefore therapy length.

Thrombophilic defectAnnual risk of first DVTRelative risk vs controlsRisk of recurrence
Antithrombin deficiency · protein C deficiency · protein S deficiency1.52–1.90%15–19×At 5 years 40%; at 10 years 55%

Slide 33 — Risk stratification. The anticoagulant-protein deficiencies (red) carry an order of magnitude more risk than factor V Leiden (yellow).

🪝 The clinically important asymmetry

Compare the two rows. Losing a brake (antithrombin, protein C, protein S) gives a relative risk of 15–19×. Pushing the accelerator (factor V Leiden, prothrombin G20210A) gives only 3–5×. Factor V Leiden is by far the most common thrombophilia and by no means the most dangerous one — which is exactly why finding it in a patient with a provoked clot rarely changes management.

⚠️ Why thrombophilia testing in the acute period is unreliable

Factor and protein levels are affected by many conditions. The lecture lists each trap:

SituationEffect on testing
PregnancyAlters multiple factor and protein levels
Acute period and inflammationElevated factor 8 and fibrinogen
HeparinDecreases antithrombin III levels
WarfarinDecreases protein C and protein S levels
The thrombosis itselfAntithrombin III and proteins C and S may be consumed by the clot
Lupus anticoagulantMay be transient — hence the 12-week repeat requirement

Genetic testing may be run at any time — DNA does not change with acute illness or drugs. That is the one exception, and it is why factor V Leiden and prothrombin G20210A are tested by molecular methods.

The recommendation: wait several months after the thrombotic episode to evaluate fully, and if possible, off anticoagulation.

🩺 Lecture summary — the closing slide
  • Several abnormalities increase thrombosis risk: decreased anticoagulant proteins (antithrombin, proteins C and S) and increased procoagulant proteins (mutated factor 5, prothrombin overexpression, increased factor 8).
  • Diagnosis in the acute period may be difficult.
  • Before testing for thrombophilia, consider whether the patient has other clotting risk factors — cancer, obesity, immobility.
  • A variety of blood clotting medications are available. Therapy length should be based on risk factors and risk of recurrence, not on the presence of a thrombophilia alone.

Q: A 28-year-old woman has a deep vein thrombosis two weeks after starting a combined oral contraceptive. Testing while she is on heparin shows a low antithrombin III level and heterozygous factor V Leiden. How should you interpret these results, and how long should she be treated?

Answer

The antithrombin result is uninterpretable. Heparin decreases antithrombin III levels, and antithrombin can also be consumed by the acute thrombosis itself. It must be repeated several months later, off anticoagulation.

The factor V Leiden result is valid, because it is genetic testing, which may be run at any time. But heterozygous factor V Leiden carries a relative risk of only 3–5× — far less than an anticoagulant-protein deficiency at 15–19× — and roughly 5% of Caucasians carry it.

Duration is set by the circumstances of the clot, not the genotype. The oral contraceptive is a minor reversible risk factor, giving about a 5% recurrence risk in the first year. Standard treatment with removal of the trigger (stopping the contraceptive) is appropriate; the factor V Leiden result does not by itself justify indefinite anticoagulation.

Q: Given that roughly 25% of the general population has some thrombophilia, why is finding one in a patient with a provoked clot rarely useful?

Answer

Because a finding that common has poor specificity — with a quarter of everyone carrying something, a positive result is close to expected and does not establish causation for this clot.

More decisively, the result does not change management. Duration of anticoagulation is driven by the recurrence risk, which is set by the circumstances: 3% after a major transient risk factor, 5% after a minor reversible one, 10% for unprovoked or persistent risk. A provoked clot sits in the low-risk group whether or not factor V Leiden is present.

This is exactly why the lecture insists on asking first: how will a positive result be used? If the answer is "it will not change therapy", the remaining justification is family counselling — and that is a separate discussion, best had months later and off anticoagulation.

Reference

Glossary and Abbreviations

Every abbreviation and technical term used in this file, written out and defined.

Thrombotic microangiopathies
TMA — thrombotic microangiopathy
Umbrella term for small-vessel thrombosis with mechanical red cell destruction. Includes TTP, HUS and aHUS.
TTP — thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura
Systemic, platelet-rich microthrombi caused by failure to degrade large von Willebrand factor multimers. Incidence 0.37 per 100,000 per year.
HUS — hemolytic uremic syndrome
Predominantly renal, platelet–fibrin-rich thrombi caused by Shiga toxin endothelial damage, classically after E. coli infection.
aHUS — atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome
HUS caused by uncontrolled complement activation — defects in factor H, factor I, membrane cofactor protein, or thrombomodulin. Treated with complement blockade.
MAHA — microangiopathic hemolytic anemia
Red cell destruction by mechanical shearing on intravascular strands, producing schistocytes.
Schistocyte
A fragmented red cell — angular, without central pallor. The morphological marker of a microangiopathy.
ADAMTS13
The protease that cleaves ultra-large von Willebrand factor multimers. Deficient (congenital) or inhibited (acquired IgG antibody) in TTP.
Weibel–Palade body
Endothelial storage granule holding von Willebrand factor. Its contents emerge as ultra-large multimers requiring ADAMTS13 trimming.
Shiga toxin
Bacterial toxin from enterohemorrhagic E. coli and Shigella dysenteriae that directly damages glomerular endothelium.
Complement factor H (CFH)
A circulating regulator of the alternative complement pathway, made in the liver. Deficiency or autoantibodies against it cause aHUS.
MCP / CD46 — membrane cofactor protein
A membrane-bound complement regulator. Because it is made by the kidney itself, aHUS from MCP mutations does better after transplantation than aHUS from circulating-factor defects.
Eculizumab
A monoclonal antibody against complement C5; the targeted therapy for aHUS.
Plasma exchange
The emergency treatment for TTP — simultaneously removes the ADAMTS13 inhibitor and replaces the enzyme.
HELLP syndrome
Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets — a pregnancy-associated microangiopathy in the "etiology not understood" group.
Thrombophilias
Thrombophilia
A hypercoagulable state. Present in roughly 25% of the general population, and in about 60% of patients presenting with a deep vein thrombosis.
Virchow's triad
The three categories of thrombosis risk: endothelial cell damage, blood stasis, and a hypercoagulable state.
VTE — venous thromboembolism
Deep vein thrombosis and/or pulmonary embolism, considered together.
DVT — deep vein thrombosis
Thrombosis of a deep vein, usually of the leg.
PE — pulmonary embolism
Embolic occlusion of a pulmonary artery, usually from a deep vein thrombosis.
Protein C deficiency
Loss of the protease that, with protein S, inactivates factors 5a and 8a. Relative risk of thrombosis 15–19×. Homozygous deficiency causes neonatal purpura fulminans.
Protein S deficiency
Cofactor for activated protein C. Appears to be worse than protein C deficiency; the two together are worse still.
Antithrombin III deficiency
Loss of the inhibitor of thrombin and factor 10a. Homozygous deficiency is not compatible with life. Because the protein is small it is easily lost through proteinuria or chest tube drainage. Causes heparin resistance.
Purpura fulminans
Rapidly progressive dermal microvascular thrombosis with skin necrosis; the neonatal presentation of homozygous protein C or S deficiency.
FVL — factor V Leiden
The most common thrombophilia (~5% of Caucasians, 20–30% of VTE). The R506Q mutation prevents deactivation of factor 5 by protein C. Relative risk 3–5×.
Activated protein C resistance
The functional consequence of factor V Leiden: factor 5a is not cleaved by activated protein C.
Prothrombin G20210A
A mutation in the 3′ untranslated region that increases pre-messenger-RNA stability and therefore prothrombin levels. Prevalence 2.3% in Caucasians, 0.5% in African-Americans.
Dysfibrinogenemia
Structurally abnormal fibrinogen. Can cause either bleeding or clotting.
Lipoprotein(a)
A lipoprotein variant listed among the acquired thrombophilias.
Antiphospholipid syndrome
APS / APLA syndrome — antiphospholipid (antibody) syndrome
An acquired thrombophilia defined by one clinical criterion (thrombosis or defined pregnancy morbidity) plus a persistent laboratory criterion.
LA — lupus anticoagulant
A double misnomer: patients need not have lupus (about 8% develop it later), and it prolongs clotting in vitro but promotes thrombosis in vivo.
Anti-cardiolipin antibody
An antiphospholipid antibody (IgG and IgM). Causes a false-positive non-treponemal test for syphilis, because those tests use a cardiolipin antigen.
Anti-β2-glycoprotein-1 antibody
An antiphospholipid antibody (IgG and IgM) included in the diagnostic criteria.
Anti-prothrombin antibody
An antiphospholipid antibody which, at high level, may cause a hemorrhagic disorder rather than thrombosis.
dRVVT — dilute Russell viper venom test
A phospholipid-dependent clotting assay used to detect a lupus anticoagulant. Prolongation that corrects with added phospholipid is confirmatory.
Mixing study
Patient plasma mixed with normal plasma. Corrects → factor deficiency; fails to correct → inhibitor. A lupus anticoagulant fails to correct.
Drugs and monitoring
Aspirin
Irreversible inhibitor of prostaglandin H synthase, blocking thromboxane A2. Effect lasts the platelet lifespan (7–10 days). First-line for mildly increased thrombosis risk.
Clopidogrel
Irreversible P2Y12 (ADP receptor) blocker. Related drugs: prasugrel, ticlopidine. Not useful when platelets are normal and other factors drive the thrombosis.
Heparin (unfractionated)
Activates antithrombin III. Monitored by aPTT (1.5–2.5× normal) or anti-factor 10a (0.3–0.7 U/mL). Hepatic clearance. Reversed by protamine sulfate.
LMWH — low-molecular-weight heparin
Enoxaparin, dalteparin. Better bioavailability, longer half-life, predictable response, generally no monitoring. Renally cleared. Lower HIT and osteoporosis risk. If monitored: anti-factor 10a 0.5–1.0 U/mL twice daily, 1.0–2.0 U/mL daily.
Fondaparinux
A pentasaccharide anticoagulant. Category B in pregnancy; 10% detected in fetal plasma. Very low risk of HIT. Renally cleared, monitored by anti-factor Xa activity.
Protamine sulfate
The reversal agent for heparin.
HIT — heparin-induced thrombocytopenia
Antibody-mediated platelet activation against the heparin–platelet factor 4 complex. A prothrombotic state despite the low platelet count. Typically days 5–14; venous:arterial thrombosis about 4:1.
PF4 — platelet factor 4
The platelet protein that binds heparin to form the antigenic complex in HIT.
SRA — serotonin release assay
A functional HIT test measuring platelet activation. Used when the immunoassay result conflicts with clinical suspicion. Negative predictive value approaches 100% when both it and the PF4 assay are negative.
4T score
Pre-test probability score for HIT: Thrombocytopenia, Timing, Thrombosis, oTher cause. 6–8 high · 4–5 intermediate · 0–3 low.
Argatroban, lepirudin
Direct thrombin inhibitors used as alternative anticoagulation in HIT, where no heparin compound and no warfarin may be used.
Warfarin
Oral vitamin K antagonist blocking factors 2, 7, 9, 10 and proteins C and S (the "1972" mnemonic). Monitored by PT/INR. Requires heparin bridging; contraindicated in pregnancy; reversed by vitamin K, fresh frozen plasma, or prothrombin complex concentrate.
Warfarin-induced skin necrosis
Dermal thrombosis in the first days of warfarin, caused by the early fall in protein C before the procoagulant factors fall. The same mechanism causes venous limb gangrene if warfarin is used alone in HIT.
DOAC — direct oral anticoagulant
Factor 10a inhibitors: rivaroxaban (Xarelto), apixaban (Eliquis), edoxaban (Savaysa), betrixaban (Bevyxxa). Direct thrombin inhibitor: dabigatran (Pradaxa).
PCC — prothrombin complex concentrate
A concentrate of the vitamin K-dependent factors, used to reverse warfarin rapidly.
OCP / HRT
Oral contraceptive pill / hormone replacement therapy. A minor reversible risk factor with a relative risk of about 4×.
TAFI — thrombin-activatable fibrinolysis inhibitor
A protein whose elevation is not an independent risk factor for venous thrombosis.

🎯 Coagulation II — High-Yield One-Pager

Cyril Jacquot, MD, PhD · condensed by learning objective — LO1 microangiopathies · LO2 thrombophilias · LO3 anticoagulants · LO4 risk stratification

LO 1 · TMA

Mechanistic split

  • TTP = cannot degrade large VWF multimers (ADAMTS13) → systemic, platelet-rich
  • HUS = Shiga toxin endothelial damage (E. coli) → renal, platelet–fibrin
  • aHUS = factor H deficiency / complement activation
  • Drugs + transplant → features of both

TTP mechanism

  • Weibel–Palade bodies release ultra-large VWF
  • ADAMTS13 normally trims them
  • Congenital deficiency or IgG inhibitor → uncleaved
  • Platelets seized → thrombocytopenia + MAHA
  • Rx plasma exchange — replaces enzyme + removes antibody; no platelet transfusion
  • Acquired (antibody) presents 20s–30s; congenital much earlier
  • 0.37 per 100,000/yr

aHUS

  • Alternative pathway continually on
  • Defects: CFH, factor I, MCP/CD46, thrombomodulin
  • MAC destroys own endothelium → exposes TF/collagen → clot
  • Rx eculizumab (anti-C5)
  • Test genetics before renal transplant — recurrence is high

★ The discriminator

  • All TMAs: PT/aPTT normal, fibrinogen normal
  • DIC: both prolonged, fibrinogen falls
  • Schistocytes in all — the coag panel separates them
LO 2 · THROMBOPHILIA

Two mechanisms only

  • Lost brake: protein C, protein S, antithrombin III → RR 15–19×
  • Pushed accelerator: factor V Leiden, prothrombin G20210A → RR 3–5×
  • Common ≠ dangerous

Key numbers

  • FVL: 5% Caucasians, 20–30% of VTE, R506Q, resists protein C
  • Prothrombin G20210A: 2.3% Caucasian, 0.5% African-American; 3′ UTR → more mRNA stability
  • Antithrombin: <0.5%; homozygous lethal; lost in proteinuria → heparin resistance
  • Protein S worse than C; homozygous → neonatal purpura fulminans

Antiphospholipid syndrome

  • Double misnomer: not lupus (8% later); prolongs in vitro, clots in vivo
  • Mix fails to correct; corrects with extra phospholipid
  • Tests: aPTT, dRVVT, anti-cardiolipin, anti-β2-GP1
  • Anti-cardiolipin → false-positive syphilis
  • Criteria: thrombosis or 3 losses <10wk / 1 loss ≥10wk / 1 birth <34wk, plus persistence 12 weeks apart
LO 3–4 · DRUGS & RISK

Platelets vs factors

  • Platelets: aspirin (irreversible COX), clopidogrel (P2Y12)
  • Factors: heparin, warfarin, DOACs
  • Arterial = platelet-rich; venous = fibrin-rich

Heparins

  • UFH: activates antithrombin III; aPTT 1.5–2.5×, anti-Xa 0.3–0.7; hepatic; protamine
  • ★ Only a long tail bridges antithrombin→thrombin; factor 10a needs no bridge → short chains = anti-Xa only
  • LMWH: predictable, no monitoring, renal, anti-Xa 0.5–1.0 (BID) / 1.0–2.0 (daily)
  • Fondaparinux: pentasaccharide, very low HIT, cat B, 10% fetal

HIT — prothrombotic!

  • Days 5–14; >50% fall or <100k; venous:arterial 4:1
  • 4T: 6–8 high, 4–5 intermediate, 0–3 low
  • Anti-heparin/PF4 immunoassay, then SRA if mismatch
  • Rx argatroban / lepirudin
  • Avoid: warfarin alone (gangrene), LMWH (cross-reacts), no anticoagulation
  • High 4T → treat · low → DON'T test · intermediate → test

Warfarin & DOACs

  • Warfarin: "1972" = factors 2, 7, 9, 10 + proteins C, S; PT/INR
  • Bridge — protein C falls first; contraindicated in pregnancy
  • Reverse: vitamin K, FFP, PCC
  • "-xaban" = factor Xa; dabigatran = thrombin
  • DOACs: no routine monitoring, rapid onset, fewer interactions; cost, no antidote, hard to monitor

★ Recurrence risk = duration

  • Major transient (surgery, bedrest) → 3%/yr
  • Minor reversible (OCP, flight) → 5%/yr
  • Unprovoked / persistent → 10%/yr
  • Test if: family history, <45 yrs, no risk factors, recurrent, unusual site (mesenteric, upper limb, cerebral sinus)
  • Only test if the result changes what you do; genetics = any time, once
  • Antibodies without the syndrome are not anticoagulated
  • Heparin ↓antithrombin · warfarin ↓protein C/S · acute ↑factor 8 → wait months, off anticoagulation. Genetic testing any time.
